source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Confidence-weighted voting over one model's own samples beats plain voting at equal sample count. How the confidence is made matters a lot. Within-question normalisation (softmax with tuned temperature) is needed. The best-calibrated confidence method was not the best for voting.
numbers: 9 models, 4 datasets (GSM8K 1,320 questions; MATH 5K; MMLU-Pro 5K sampled; BBH). Cost reduction vs plain self-consistency, budget 5 / budget 10 samples: P(True) 41% / 46% (plain vote needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10); response probability 22% / 31%; verbal 0-100 22% / 30%; verbal binary 18% / 10%. Accuracy gain at the same budget is small, about 1 to 2 points for P(True) (table layout partly garbled). Without normalisation P(True) saves 32% at budget 10, with it 46%. Within-question discrimination (WQD): P(True) 62.3%, response prob 59.0%, verbal 0-100 56.1%, verbal binary 52.2%. Calibration error (ECE-t) ranks them differently.
quote: Notably, the best-calibrated confidence method was the least effective for CISC.
limits: Gains are mostly in samples saved, not in accuracy at a fixed budget. Needs a tuned softmax temperature per method. P(True) costs an extra call per sample. Math and MMLU-Pro style tasks with a single parsed answer.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: verbal 0-100 weighting helps modestly (-30% samples), P(True) more (-46%). Judge a confidence signal by how well it ranks right vs wrong samples of the same question, not by calibration. In code: weight each vote by softmax(confidence/T); fall back to the plain vote if the signal cannot rank samples (see Sakai, d05).

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling once the leader's lead over the other answers is statistically safe (Dirichlet model of answer counts). Agreement share is a cheap gate: easy items stop early, hard items get more samples, with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models (GPT-3.5-turbo, Vicuna-13B, Codex), max 40 samples at temperature 0.7. Math: 73.2 -> 73.1 accuracy with 40 -> 13.8 samples (3.3x fewer). Commonsense 66.0 -> 65.8 with 15.8 samples. Symbolic 72.8 -> 72.8 with 13.1. Code 35.2 -> 35.6 with 173.6 vs 312.5 samples. By model: GPT-3.5 76.4 -> 76.2 with 10.0 samples (4.4x); Vicuna-13B 54.0 -> 54.1 with 21.7 samples (1.9x). Best case 7.9x fewer samples. Average accuracy change under 0.1.
limits: This gates sampling cost, not correctness. It tests whether the current lead is stable, not whether the modal answer is right. It does not detect items where the model is confidently wrong. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: agreement share is good enough to decide how many samples to draw. It is not shown to decide when to abstain. Use the lead test as the stopping rule in S7 to save tokens, and escalate (verifier, tool) when the lead stays small at the cap.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-High Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sampling in small windows and stopping when a window is unanimous cuts samples by 34% to 84% with comparable accuracy.
numbers: Sample reductions from the abstract: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; per-model accuracy tables not extracted. Reasoning tasks with a single answer.
agent_relevance: Second independent source that agreement-based early stopping is safe on reasoning tasks (gap 3). Same limit as d02: it measures stability, not truth.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency, consistency vs accuracy analysis
finding: The share of sampled paths that agree with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K, so low agreement is a usable 'I do not know' signal.
numbers: Figure 5 on GSM8K; the text gives no single number, only 'highly correlated'. Imperfect-prompt test: LaMDA-137B 17.1 -> 14.9 with an imperfect chain of thought, 23.4 with self-consistency over 40 paths.
quote: consistency ... is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: Correlation across items, shown as a figure only. No threshold, no per-bin accuracy table, no test of items where agreement is high but wrong. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports using modal share as a rough confidence. A threshold must be fitted on the agent's own data. Not enough on its own to gate abstention.

source: Sakai, Song, Larson (2026) When Does Delegation Beat Majority? (PPV)
finding: On one small model sampled 128 times per question, a label-free aggregator that uses per-group answer entropy and reasoning-embedding similarity overturns some wrong majorities. It beats plain vote by 1.5 points. Same-model P(True) was below chance as a confidence signal.
numbers: Qwen3-1.7B, temperature 1.5, MMLU-Pro test 12,032 questions, 16 voters (groups of 8 samples). Accuracy all questions / non-trivial (n=8,099): best single voter 35.78%; majority 40.71% / 28.00%; PPV with confidence 42.21% / 30.24% (+2.24); PPV 'div' 41.92% / 29.83%; oracle pass@16 44.68% / 33.93%. Paired test: PPV right and majority wrong 366, majority right and PPV wrong 185, p about 1e-14. Per-disagreement precision: 'div' mode 82.7% (187 of 226), confidence mode 66.4%. P(True) AUROC 0.47; top-25% P(True) voters correct 32.1% vs base rate 35.4%. A selector to pick the mode per question did not beat the best single mode (100-question pilot).
limits: One small RL-tuned model, one benchmark, multiple-choice letters, embeddings needed. Gain closes about 38% of the gap to oracle. Polarity (low entropy = reliable) flips on some questions and could not be detected without labels. The theory is a two-option model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 4, 9, 10: within one model's own samples a wrong majority can sometimes be overturned (366 vs 185 net wins), but only by about 1.5 to 2 points and with extra machinery. Do not use P(True) as the weight for a small model. Treat any flip-to-minority rule as a measured, tested component, not a default.

source: Kurvers et al. (2016) Boosting medical diagnostics by pooling independent judgments (PNAS)
finding: Pooling independent doctors beats the best doctor only when the doctors' accuracy is similar. Reopened from the PMC full text this session: numbers confirmed.
numbers: Breast cancer: 16,813 diagnoses by 101 radiologists on 182 mammograms; mean sensitivity 0.766 (SD 0.112), specificity 0.665 (SD 0.113). Skin cancer: 4,320 diagnoses by 40 dermatologists on 108 lesions; mean sensitivity 0.833 (SD 0.130). Pairs combined with a confidence rule, triplets with majority rule. Both rules beat the better member only when |delta Youden J| < 0.1; otherwise the better member won. Both rules always beat the average member.
limits: Radiology and dermatology, human experts with confidence ratings. The 0.1 gap in Youden's J is a descriptive cut, not a law.
agent_relevance: Closes the Kurvers part of gap 8 (claim K20 now verified for this study). For an agent: pooling helps when the samples are about equally good; if one prompt or tool is clearly better, do not average it with weaker ones.

source: Lorenz et al. (2011) How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect (PNAS)
finding: Letting people see others' estimates narrowed the spread without making the group more accurate. Reopened from PMC: the 21.3% figure is real and belongs to Lorenz (arithmetic mean closer than individuals in only 21.3% of cases).
numbers: 144 ETH Zurich students, 12 sessions of 12, 6 factual questions, 5 rounds, real payments. In only 21.3% of cases is the arithmetic mean closer to the truth than the individual first estimates (right-skewed answers). In log space the mean is closer in 77.1% of cases. First-estimate aggregates vs truth: population density true 184, arithmetic mean 2,644 (+1,337.2%), geometric mean 132 (-28.1%), median 130 (-29.3%); new immigrants to Zurich true 10,067, arithmetic 26,773 (+165.9%), geometric 8,178 (-18.8%), median 10,000 (-0.7%); assaults true 9,272, arithmetic 135,051 (+1,356.5%), geometric 6,039 (-34.9%), median 4,000 (-56.9%). Three effects: social influence (diversity falls, collective error barely changes), range reduction (truth moves to the edge of the estimate range), confidence boost.
quote: In only 21.3% of the cases is the arithmetic mean closer to the truth than the individual first estimates.
limits: Estimation tasks with ordinary students and moderate-difficulty questions. Not a vote on a discrete answer. Questions chosen to have skewed distributions.
agent_relevance: Settles the duplicate 21.3%: it is Lorenz (b02 correct). For numeric outputs from samples use the median or geometric mean (log space), not the arithmetic mean, when errors are skewed. Keep samples blind to each other (G4).

source: Prelec, Seung, McCoy (2017) A solution to the single-question crowd wisdom problem (Nature)
finding: Only the abstract and a preview could be read (paywall). The rule is: pick the answer that is more popular than people predicted. The 21.3% error-cut figure in entry b27 could not be checked, so it stays unverified.
numbers: Preview text only: simulations show a majority of 90% is correct about 90% of the time, while a majority of 55% is not much better than chance. No study-level error numbers were visible.
quote: select the answer that is more popular than people predict
limits: Full text blocked. The result needs respondents who differ in information, and predictions of the crowd that mean something.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open for Prelec. Gap 9: the principle needs an informed minority. In one model's samples there is no private information, so the premise is not met. It stays untested.

source: Naik et al. (2024) Diversity of Thought Improves Reasoning Abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Varying the approach named in the prompt (method of elimination, finite state machine, etc.) gives far more useful diversity than temperature sampling of one prompt. Temperature-only self-consistency barely moved the hard planning tasks.
numbers: GPT-4, zero-shot CoT. Graph colouring: CoT 15.0, SC-10 23.0, in-call diverse prompts (IDIV-SE) 74.0, diverse prompts across calls (DIV-SE) 97.0. Blocksworld 3: 70, 73, 82, 94. Blocksworld 4/5: 40.0, 41.2, 57.0, 69.6. AQuA-RAT: DIV-SE +9.84 (few-shot, base 71.9) and +14.6 (zero-shot, base 70.47) points for GPT-4. Table 5 (AQuA few-shot): majority vote 79.90 vs meta-reasoning 79.24 for GPT-4; 64.47 vs 67.70 for GPT-3.5. Temperature 0.7. Authors say DIV-SE is Pareto-better on cost.
limits: Gains are largest on tasks where the prompt strategy matters a lot (planning, colouring). Cost figures are the authors' own. Mixes diversity with better individual prompts: single approach prompts scored well above plain CoT alone (for example +13.8 to +16.8 on Blocksworld 4/5).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (part): temperature samples of one prompt differ little; changing the method in the prompt raises both diversity and accuracy. For S7 draw samples from several method prompts, but credit part of the gain to better prompts, not only to lower correlation.

source: Fadnavis, Kanakaraj, Wyss (2026) Beyond Consensus: Trace-Level Synthesis in Mixture of Agents (SC-MoA)
finding: With one model and paraphrased inputs, an LLM aggregator that reads the full reasoning traces beat plain voting at about equal call count, even when all samples agreed. Sub-step content from minority chains is the active ingredient. This is the closest measured case for premise-level over answer-level aggregation.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b, 5 paraphrased inputs, SC-MoA 11 calls vs SC k=10 (10 calls). BBH-3 (n=296): SC 80.4 vs SC-MoA 86.5 (+6.1). AIME (n=90): 85.6 vs 91.1. LCB-Hard (n=171): 57.3 vs 62.6. GPQA-Diamond (n=198) SC-MoA 73.2. Pre-refinement synthesis vs voting at consensus: GPQA 12 beneficial vs 5 harmful flips (+3.5 pp, McNemar p=0.09); BBH-3 16 vs 5 (+3.7 pp, p=0.016). Over BBH, GPQA, AIME (n=575): 81 beneficial vs 4 harmful flips after anchored refinement. Ablation: answer-only and majority-only inputs fall back to the vote baseline; showing only minority proposals keeps the full gain (73.2, flip ratio 2.75). On LCB-Hard 69% of problems were unanimous, yet always aggregating beat gating by 5.1 pp, and 48.3% of unanimous test-pass clusters hid divergence on hidden tests.
limits: Single paper, single generator model, preprint; 7 of 12 pairwise McNemar tests at p<0.05, the rest on GPQA and LCB-Hard. Call counts are matched but token counts for reading all traces are higher. An LLM, not code, does the aggregating, which fits the rule 'aggregate in code' (G5) poorly.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: partial answer. Reading sub-steps beats counting final answers at about equal calls, but nobody has measured a doctrinal-paradox rate or compared premise-wise code voting. Test it in our harness: premise-wise code vote vs answer vote vs LLM trace reader. Weakens claim K16 (LLM aggregator no better than code) for reasoning tasks.

source: Fadnavis et al. (2026) SC-MoA appendix K: error correlation with personas vs identical prompts
finding: Persona prompts did not lower the correlation between samples' errors. Error correlation among five samples from one model stays about 0.6 whether they use five persona prompts or one prompt.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b, N=5. Mean pairwise error correlation, persona-diverse vs i.i.d.: GPQA-Diamond 0.633 [0.557, 0.705] vs 0.603 [0.522, 0.679]; LCB-Hard 0.571 [0.491, 0.648] vs 0.607 [0.536, 0.676]. Main text: error correlations statistically identical between perturbation and standard sampling. Perturbation content ablation (GPQA / LCB-Hard): hand-crafted personas 72.7 / 63.7; paraphrased CoT 72.7 / 65.9; GPT-generated strategies 70.2 / 60.8; McNemar p>0.25 for all pairs.
limits: Two benchmarks, N=5, wide intervals, one reasoning model. Error correlation of about 0.6 on hard problems is high.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a direct measurement. With r about 0.6, five samples are worth roughly 1.5 independent voters (design effect 1+(n-1)r gives n_eff = 5/3.4 = 1.5). That arithmetic is mine, from their r; they do not report it. Persona or paraphrase diversity did not fix it here.

source: Hu and Collier (2024) Quantifying the Persona Effect in LLM Simulations
finding: Persona variables explain little variance in human annotations, and persona prompting gives modest gains that are largest where annotators disagree mildly.
numbers: Persona variables account for under 10% of annotation variance in existing subjective NLP datasets. A 70B model with persona prompting, zero-shot, captures 81% of the variance a linear regression trained on ground-truth annotations can reach.
limits: About simulating human annotators, not about getting right answers. Subjective tasks without a true label. Low direct relevance.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 (weak): persona prompting adds a small, task-dependent spread of outputs. Do not count on personas as a source of independent judgments.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: At matched budget, chain-of-thought self-consistency beats multi-agent debate and Reflexion on most tasks. Debate gets worse or plateaus as the budget grows, because answer diversity falls from round to round.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Budget cap 20 queries or 10k tokens: CoT-SC 20 samples; debate 6 agents x 3 rounds = 18 queries; Reflexion 10 trials (19 queries). Datasets: GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, CSQA, HotpotQA, Game of 24. SC rises smoothly with budget. Debate plateaus or declines with more budget. Answer entropy falls each debate round; SC entropy does not. Plan-and-Solve SC beat CoT-SC only on HotpotQA. Tree of Thoughts beat SC on Game of 24 only with a strong model (GPT-4).
limits: Older models. No headline accuracy table was extracted, only the budget curves and text. Debate was run in the original MAD form.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: strong, earlier evidence that debate needs an equal-budget SC control. Dependent sampling (reading peers) cuts diversity, which cuts the vote's value (G4).

source: Ferreira, Liu, Zheng (2026) Beyond Symmetric Agents: Cognitive Diversity and Multi-Agent Debate in Small Language Models
finding: With 23 small models, five tasks and more than 5,500 runs, debate beat single-agent answers by 3 to 7 points but only tied or lost to a budget-matched majority vote over independent samples. Persona prompts lowered accuracy.
numbers: Mean over four inline-scored tasks: solo 80.4, debate (3 agents x 3 rounds) 84.4, SC-9 (9 samples, majority vote) 84.8, persona debate 81.9. Debate vs solo: GSM8K +3.3, MMLU +6.6, CSQA +5.7 points (p<0.002). Versus SC-9: no difference on math, GSM8K, MMLU; on CSQA SC-9 wins by 2.3 pp (p=0.011). Debate cost 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x total tokens (generated tokens 1.06x; the rest is re-reading peers' transcripts). Mixed-model teams lost to majority votes over their own rosters by 1.04 points (80 teams, replicated at a second seed). Nearly all of debate's gain arrives in the first exchange. Context-window overflow in transcripts moved debate vs sampling from -1.8 points to parity.
limits: Small open-weight models (0.6B to 32B); 100 problems per task; one seed for the main grid. Debate may do better on tasks with more headroom or with trained debaters.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the best equal-budget test so far, and it supports 'vote, do not debate' for one model. Also gap 2: the diversity levers (persona, temperature, model identity) did not beat plain independent sampling. Watch token accounting: equal generations are not equal tokens.

source: Mansuri et al. (2026) Multi-agent discussion gains less when dissent is withheld
finding: A small model of agent behaviour explains when discussion beats voting: discussion can overturn a wrong initial majority only when the rate of withholding dissent is below a critical rate. The gain shrinks as withholding rises across LLMs.
numbers: Four behaviours: withhold dissent, internalise a stated answer, reconsider after seeing dissent, correct towards the truth. Tested on HiddenBench and MedEInst (MuSiQue unclear), 8 or more LLMs. Forcing withholding to 1 nearly removed the gain; instructing agents not to withhold raised it; turning reasoning off raised it because reasoning raises internalisation.
limits: Preprint. Rates estimated from conversation logs with a Bayesian method. No single headline accuracy number extracted. Hidden-profile discussion tasks, not plain voting.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: explains why debate and vote results conflict. A voting-only design avoids the conformity problem. If a discussion step is added, the minority must be forced to state dissent.

source: Wen et al. (2026) Test-Time Scaling of Divergent-Convergent Reasoning (DCR)
finding: One reviewer-style reconciliation step over a model's own proposals can recover the correct answer when it is only in the minority, a case where plain vote fails.
numbers: Table 1, single-round DCR with 25 reviewer calls, trial accuracy sampling -> DCR(self): MATH500 GPT-OSS 83.9 -> 84.6; Llama-4 36.4 -> 73.7; Llama-3.3 20.8 -> 51.4; Granite-4 26.2 -> 53.3. AIME 2024 GPT-OSS 74.3 -> 88.1; Llama-4 5.1 -> 29.3. Majority-vote column AIME 2024 GPT-OSS 76.7 (sampling) -> 90.0 (DCR). Recursive DCR 93.3% on AIME 2024 and 92.0% on AIME 2025 with about 27% less compute than fixed baselines. Higher dispersion of proposals goes with larger DCR gains.
limits: Math only. The huge jumps for weaker models are suspicious (for example Llama-4 36.4 -> 73.7); formatting or answer-extraction effects may be involved and were not checked. Compute parity is claimed at one point only. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: an LLM reconciler can rescue minority-correct answers, with the same caveat as d10: a model, not code, does the flip. Needs a harm count (right-to-wrong flips) before use.

source: He et al. (2026) Minority Sentinel (re-read this session)
finding: Numbers in c22 re-checked in the PDF text: they match. In a three-vendor debate setting the minority is right in a quarter of 2:1 splits, and a trained flip rule gains little.
numbers: 1,754 questions, 6 benchmarks; 686 (39.1%) had a 2:1 split; in 175 (25.5%) the minority was correct. Vote accuracy 74.3%, oracle 84.3% (10.0 point margin). Sentinel net gain +1.71 points, flip precision 81.2% (39 correct flips, 9 wrong), recovery 22.3% (39 of 175). Always trusting the minority: net -19.16%.
limits: Three different vendor models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5) after a debate, not one model's independent samples. Small classifier trained on 686 items with cross-validation.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: confirms the 25.5%. Blind flipping is very harmful (-19 points). A safe flip needs a trained, tested gate and still recovers only about a fifth of the possible gain. For one model's samples see d05 (+1.5 points).

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal Self-Consistency for LLM Generation (USC)
finding: Asking the model to pick the most consistent of its own samples works on free-form tasks where counting is impossible, and is about as good as exact-match voting where both apply. It does not scale to many samples.
numbers: Math, accuracy SC vs USC: first block GSM8K 90.4 vs 90.2 and MATH 37.9 vs 37.4 (greedy 85.7 / 30.8); second block GSM8K 78.5 vs 77.8, MATH 38.0 vs 38.1 (greedy 73.4 / 33.2). ARCADE code 45.6 (execution-based SC) vs 45.5 (USC). TruthfulQA GPT-judge, first block: greedy 62.1, USC 67.7 (informativeness 95.1 -> 99.0); second block 79.8 -> 82.5. USC does not improve GSM8K at 16 samples vs 8. USC-SC match ratio falls from 8 to 16 samples.
limits: Which block belongs to which model (PaLM 2-L, gpt-3.5-turbo) is ambiguous in the extracted text. Long contexts limit the number of samples. Order bias tested only by shuffling.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a model-as-selector is a fair fallback outside math and code, close to code voting where both work. It cannot beat a true checker. Use it only where no exact-match key exists.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2026) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Outside code and math a verifier ensemble can clearly beat majority vote, but only a weighted ensemble of many verifiers with a labelled dev set. A plain average of reward models or judges does not.
numbers: Generator Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, 100 samples per question, 33 reward models and LLM judges as verifiers. Averages over MATH500, GPQA Diamond, MMLU College, MMLU Pro: first sample 68.4; majority vote of 100 about 72.2 (Table 1; Table 3 gives 71.6 and a different GPQA entry, so the paper disagrees with itself); highest-scoring reward model 66.9 to 69.1; naive ensemble of top-10 reward models about 71.6; Weaver 87.7 (MATH 93.4, GPQA 72.1, MMLU College 94.9, MMLU Pro 90.2); pass@100 ceiling 91.9; o3-mini first sample 86.7. Weaver beats majority by 15.5 and the naive ensemble by 17.1 points. Oracle-weighted ensembles beat naive ones by up to 11.2 points. With only 0.01n labelled samples, accuracy drops 20.1% on average from the oracle-weighted case. Llama 3.1 8B: majority 57.2 -> Weaver 70.0 average.
limits: Weights come from a labelled dev subset or weak supervision on the test distribution. Table 1 layout is garbled in the extract, so some per-dataset cells are inferred. A 33-model verifier pool is costly (a distilled 400M model keeps 98.7% of the accuracy). Benchmarks are still multiple-choice or math.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: yes, a verifier ensemble can beat voting on GPQA and MMLU-style tasks (GPQA about 47 -> 72), but a single judge or a plain average will not. For an agent with one model, a verifier must be a different check (tool, test, retrieval), not the same model re-reading its answer.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
finding: A verifier with a false-positive rate caps what resampling can achieve. Weaker models have higher false-positive rates, so more samples cannot make them match a stronger model. Optimal sample count is often below 10.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+ with the original unit tests as the verifier, 200 samples per task (1,000 for Command Light). Llama-3.1, Code Llama, Command, GPT-4o. False-positive probability falls linearly with single-sample accuracy across families. With a cost of a false positive 4 times the benefit of a correct answer, optimal K is about 5 for all four models; at high enough cost the optimum is zero. Task difficulty is bimodal; false-positive rate rises with K for Llama-3.1-70B but less for Code Llama and Command.
limits: Code only, with human-written unit tests of limited coverage. They note LLM-written tests are an open question.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: a verifier helps only if its false-positive rate is low. A weak checker applied to many samples lets wrong answers through and adds a new failure mode. Cap resampling; log false positives.

source: Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne, Jose, Winkler (2018) Bayesian Ensembles of Binary-Event Forecasts: When Is It Appropriate to Extremize or Anti-Extremize?
finding: Extremizing the average is right when forecasters rely on private information, because each forecast double-counts the prior. When forecasters share information it can be right to anti-extremize (make the aggregate less extreme).
numbers: Theory plus two public datasets (Fannie Mae and Carvana loan data; three base models, 10-fold cross-validation). The best ensemble put most weight on the best base model (XGBoost) and was nearly linear over most of the range. They state the result matches the empirical finding of Tetlock and Gardner (2015) for forecasters with shared information.
limits: Not a language-model paper. Datasets are machine-learning probability models, not human or LLM forecasters. Exact scores were not extracted from the table.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: samples from one model share almost all information (error correlation about 0.6, see d11). By this theory the right default is no extremizing, or even anti-extremizing, unlike the crowd case. Test mean vs median vs log-odds with extremizing factor 1 as the default on the agent's own probability outputs.

source: Revalor, Rehman, Pal (2026) Can We Trust LLM's Logic? Graph Reasoning Coherence and Graph Self-Consistency
finding: Final-answer voting hides unfaithful reasoning. Picking the sample whose reasoning is most central in a graph of steps lowers nominal accuracy in small models but raises the share of correct answers that have faithful reasoning.
numbers: Share of wins that are faithful: MedQA SC-only wins 40% faithful (60% spurious) vs 100% for graph-selected-only wins; GPQA SC-only wins entirely spurious, graph method recovers 25%; BoolQ SC 18% vs 56%. For one strong reasoning model on GPQA, faithful share 24% for SC-only wins vs 45%. Overall 79.5% faithful wins vs 57.6% for SC (+21.9 pp, p<0.05, Wilcoxon). Their uncertainty score correlated negatively with faithfulness in 14 of 15 settings.
limits: Faithfulness is judged by their own pipeline; small models; accuracy for the graph method is lower or equal in compact models. Not a doctrinal-paradox measure, but the nearest thing: right conclusion, bad premises.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: evidence that the final-answer vote can be right for wrong reasons (a conclusion-premise mismatch). Supports checking sub-claims, but does not show that premise-wise voting improves final accuracy.

source: Shinitzky et al. (2022) Exploiting meta-cognitive features for ML-based one-shot group-decision aggregation
finding: A learned aggregator that uses each respondent's confidence and the group's meta-cognitive data raised the success rate above rule-based methods, including majority, confidence and the Surprisingly Popular Option.
numbers: 2,490 human responses over several tasks. Reported success-rate increase of 20% to 35% over standard rule-based methods (abstract).
limits: Abstract-level read only. Human crowds, not LLMs. Trained on the same data distribution; success rate, not per-item accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the only SP-adjacent result found. No paper was found that applies the Surprisingly Popular rule to a single LLM's samples; the gap stays open.

source: Abdallah et al. (2026) Large Language Models Systematically Favor Popular Options (PopMCQ)
finding: LLMs choose well-known but wrong options over less-known correct ones, with confidence staying high. This is the failure mode the Surprisingly Popular rule is designed for.
numbers: 22 open-source LLMs (0.5B to 32B). When all distractors are more popular than the correct option, models choose popular wrong answers 66% of the time. A debiasing step gained up to 54.1 accuracy points under strong popularity pressure.
limits: Entity popularity in multiple choice, not sampling dynamics. Debiasing needs a calibration split.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: indirect support that the modal sample can be the popular but wrong answer. In S7, a modal answer that is also the most obvious one deserves a second look. Still no direct SP test on samples.
